scenes.title: .gitignore & Repository Hygiene
scenes.narration: A .gitignore file tells Git which files to leave untracked, keeping your repository clean and safe from accidental leaks.

scenes.title: What to Ignore
bullets: Secrets like .env files and credentials must never be committed.
Generated artifacts such as __pycache__ and build folders add only noise.
Large data files and virtual environments bloat the repo and belong elsewhere.
scenes.narration: The most important things to ignore are secrets, because a committed API key can be exploited even after you delete it. Generated files like Python caches and build output add clutter without value, so they stay out. Large datasets and virtual environments also do not belong in Git, since they bloat clones and are better recreated from configuration.

scenes.title: A Typical .gitignore
scenes.narration: Each line is a pattern Git matches against file paths. Naming .env and pem files keeps credentials out of history. The Python section ignores caches, compiled files, and the virtual environment, while the data section uses wildcards to skip bulky CSV and parquet files. Comments starting with a hash keep the file organized and readable.

scenes.text: Add .gitignore before your first commit — once a secret is in history, ignoring it later doesn't remove it from the past.
scenes.narration: Set up .gitignore at the very start of a project. Ignoring a file only affects the future, so a secret already committed lives on in the history until you scrub it out deliberately.
